summary: The CX-80 P50e is the stretched three-row version of the CX-60 plug-in hybrid, using the same 2.5-litre petrol four, 17.8kWh (gross) battery and 241kW/500Nm combined output in a body long enough for seven seats, or six with the Azami SP's second-row captain's chairs. Reviewers praise the cabin quality, the strong performance and a genuinely usable third row, but are consistent that the electric range is modest for the money and the boot behind row three is small; a July 2026 price cut of $7,650-$8,687 reset the four-grade range downward, and the prices still stood in November 2026. Opinion splits on ride: Chasing Cars' launch drive found the PHEV more compliant than the diesel, while local testers still find the ride firm over sharp bumps on 20-inch wheels and the steering heavy around town.
pros: Now $68,100-$85,300 list after Mazda cut CX-80 PHEV prices by $7,650-$8,687 in July 2026, putting the P50e just $5,000 above the equivalent G40e petrol or D50e diesel six

Every grade posts 2.7L/100km and 64g/km on the combined cycle, so all four clear both the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficient LCT test and Victoria's 120g/km green-duty ceiling — the $85,300 Azami SP pays no LCT as a result
The battery sits under the floor, so the 258L/566L/1971L boot figures are the same as the petrol and diesel CX-80 — no cargo penalty for the plug, and braked towing stays at 2500kg
241kW/500Nm makes it the quickest CX-80 (about 7 seconds to 100km/h), and the Azami SP's ventilated second-row captain's chairs make a genuine six-seat option
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, and the high-voltage battery is covered separately for eight years
cons: 60km WLTP electric range (Mazda's 65km is the older ADR figure) is short for a $68k-plus PHEV — The Beep expects 55-60km in the real world and says you need to plug it in every night, otherwise you're driving a heavy, expensive petrol SUV

With the battery flat it is a 2237kg seven-seater on a 2.5-litre atmo four: WLTP rates it at 8.0L/100km battery-empty and GoAuto averaged 7.8L/100km over a week, roughly three times the 2.7L/100km label, so the case collapses for anyone without home charging
Only 258L behind the third row, and there is no spare wheel — just a tyre repair kit
AC charging only at 7.2kW with no DC capability, so a depleted battery needs about 2.5 hours on a wallbox and cannot be topped up usefully on a road trip

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and the GT at $75,100 sits $100 above the $75,000 cap that will matter for FBT purposes from 2027 — the Touring at $68,100 is the only grade with clear air beneath it
